Female share of secondary education enrollment across low–middle income countries in 2018 (top) vs. 2021 (bottom), ordered by infant mortality rate (per 1,000 live births). Each bar displays the proportion of secondary students who are female versus male. The dashed line marks the 45% female-share threshold to highlight countries falling below this benchmark.

</figcaption>

</figure>

The visualization compares the female share of secondary education completion rates across low to middle income countries in the years 2018 (top) and 2021 (bottom) and is ordered by infant mortality rate (per 1,000 live births) where the left of the visualization indicates low infant mortality rates and the right side indicates high reports of infant mortalities. Each bar illustrates the proportion of secondary students who are female (green) versus male (yellow). The dashed line marks the 45% female-share threshold to highlight which countries fall below this standard. The following two years, 2018 and 2021 are focused on in order to emphasize how the COVID-19 pandemic influenced secondary education completion rates in low to middle income countries and infant mortality rates. 

In the year 2018, it is important to note that the majority of countries just barely meet the 45% female share benchmark but, by 2021, almost every country in the dataset exceeded this standard. This indicates that access and retention of girls in secondary education greatly improved in the year 2021 following the height of the global pandemic which called for an emphasis on the importance of education, whether that be virtual or in person. Also visualized by the year 2021 is that the country Sierra Leone had the highest infant mortality rate and it actually becomes the country with the most share of secondary completion by females. This demonstrates a huge jump from 2018 where we see that secondary completion rates by females were at 49.5%. This suggests that progress was made in both female health and education fields following the global pandemic, especially due to the high mortality rates that it caused, and awareness that it shed on preventative health care. 

Additionally, while hovering over each bar we also can see the exact infant mortality rate for each country and note that the maximum infant mortality rate for Cabo Verde has actually decreased from 58.2% to 54.0% after the pandemic. This could be due to a greater spotlight on education in low-income countries following the outbreak of COVID-19 that would support more online work instead of in-person work that low-income countries often partake in. We also see a decline in infant mortality due to a greater focus on health that is a result of more educational opportunities and emphasis. 

We overall see a better quality of education and health for women in low-income countries following the pandemic especially due to the need for physicians and healthcare during the pandemic.
